card.hook: Picture a row of old captains' houses with their balconies hanging right out over the Aegean, as if they're waiting for the waves to drop by for a chat. That's Little Venice, and it's easy to see why guides call it the most photographed viewpoint on Mykonos.
card.stand_here: Head for the small promenade at the north end of Little Venice and look south along the row of balconies. From there you get clean, front-on shots of the houses without too much clutter.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole row of balconies and the sea into one frame. Then try 1x for a more natural look, and 2x or higher (depending on your phone) to pick out balcony and window details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and line up the balcony row with one of the horizontal lines so the houses don't lean.
card.best_time: Aim for about 45 minutes before sunset, before the promenade fills up. It gets very crowded from late afternoon in summer, so arrive early. Some people prefer sunrise for emptier streets.
card.selfie_here: Try the terrace at Bao's Cocktail Bar at sunset, which sits right on the water's edge, and stand with the Little Venice waterfront behind you. Use your front camera (or 0.5x if your front camera has it) and hold the phone a bit out and up so the houses show over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on the sea side of the low seawall outside Galleraki bar, about 20 metres south of the Caprice cocktail terrace, while you stand on the wall with the houses behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: One guide says Negrita needs a reservation after 4pm, with a minimum spend. The marble alleys in Chora can get slick after night dew, so flat soles with grip are a good idea. Take care on the uneven ground at Panagia Paraportiani too.
card.challenge: Take one shot with the balcony line sitting dead straight on a gridline, then crouch and take a second one so the sea fills more of the picture. Which one wins?
card.good_to_know: Little Venice is a row of 18th-century captains' houses with balconies over the water. The view from the promenade is free and needs no ticket, but terrace seats are separate and fill up before sunset. Kato Mili and Panagia Paraportiani are close by if you want a different angle: Kato Mili puts the windmills in front (and is often windy), while Panagia Paraportiani gives a lower angle of Little Venice with the windmills behind.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the small promenade at the north end of Little Venice and look south along the row of balconies. From there you get clean, front-on shots of the houses without too much clutter.

card.hook: Picture a row of round white towers with pointy roofs and tiny windows, sitting on a hill above the town and the sea. It's the Mykonos postcard, and your phone will love it.
card.stand_here: Stand near Μπάου, about 30 m north-east of the windmills, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. Take your wide shots from here, then walk the minute or so closer for close-ups.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to get the whole row against the sky, then try 1x for a tidier view. For one windmill, or the town below, go to 2x-5x, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Tap a white wall, then slide it a little darker so the white stays crisp in bright sun, and turn on the gridlines to keep the horizon level.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the sun is lower, gives softer light and more shape to the white walls. Those times are often calmer too, but check on the day.
card.selfie_here: Head for the open terrace at the top of the Kato Mili hill, or the gentle rise on its southern side, and stand with the mills behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if you have it, and let the windmill row and open sea fill the space over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the dirt path on the sea side of the ridge, about ten metres below the line of mills, and shoot upwards while you stand up the slope with the mills behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The seaward slope is steep in places, so wear flat shoes with good grip for the loose gravel on the ridge.
card.challenge: Take one picture where a single windmill's pointed roof looks like a hat on your head, and see who in your group spots it first.
card.good_to_know: The Venetians built most of the windmills in the 16th century, though building carried on into the early 20th century. They ground wheat and were an important source of income for local people until production stopped in the middle of the 20th century. One of them is now a museum, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near Μπάου, about 30 m north-east of the windmills, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. Take your wide shots from here, then walk the minute or so closer for close-ups.

card.hook: Picture a whole bay of umbrellas and sunbeds lined up like they're waiting for roll call. Paradise Beach looks its best from above, and the curve of the sand does most of the work for you.
card.stand_here: Head for the rocks at the edges of the bay, above the beach clubs. The phone icon on the map sits on Paradise Beach itself, so use it as your starting point. Face the bay so the whole curve of sand is in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole bay and the line of beach clubs into one shot. Then try 1x for a more natural view, and 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out a row of umbrellas.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the beach clubs or your friend on the screen, then drag the brightness down a touch so the pale sand and sky keep their detail.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning for quieter water and sand, with fewer people and less music in your photos.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold your arm out so the bay curves away behind your shoulder. If you're with friends, the rocks above the beach clubs are a good spot for portraits with the bay behind them.
card.rules_and_safety: Check on the day that the rocks are still accessible. In high season, expect crowds and music from the beach clubs.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole bay, then one close-up of a single row of umbrellas, and see which one you like better.
card.good_to_know: Paradise Beach is on the coast of Mykonos, on a bay lined with beach clubs. The sand curves around the bay, and the repeating umbrellas and sunbeds give photos lots of colour and structure. Agia Anna is a separate beach nearby.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the rocks at the edges of the bay, above the beach clubs. The phone icon on the map sits on Paradise Beach itself, so use it as your starting point. Face the bay so the whole curve of sand is in front of you.

card.hook: Picture a beach full of sunbeds, umbrellas and water sports, then a little white chapel with a red dome sitting quietly at the far end like it's got nothing to do with any of it. That's Agios Stefanos, and it's an easy one to photograph.
card.stand_here: Walk to the far end of Agios Stefanos beach, about 3.5 km from Mykonos town, and stand at the front of the chapel facing the sea. From the sand, look south to spot the chapel. Keep it in the foreground and let the bay and Delos fill the background.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the chapel with the bay and Delos behind it. Drop to 0.5x for more beach and sky. If your phone has 2x, try it for a tighter shot of the red dome against the water.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the white wall, then drag the slider down a little to make it darker, so the walls keep their detail instead of going flat.
card.best_time: Sunset is the favourite, when the light falls over the water towards Delos. Early morning or late afternoon also gives you more detail in the white walls. Skip roughly 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. in summer, when the glare washes them out.
card.selfie_here: Try the sand at the front of the red-domed chapel, at the far end of the beach. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone offers it, and hold it a little low so the chapel sits over your shoulder. Travellers have posted photos from here, but nobody has confirmed the exact framing, so test a few shots when you arrive.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand mid-beach on the sand looking towards the chapel, ideally in late afternoon with the sun behind them, while you stand at the chapel front.
card.rules_and_safety: The chapel is a small place of worship and is rarely open to visitors, so plan to photograph it from outside.
card.challenge: Take three frames of the chapel at different distances: close, halfway, and from the beach. Then pick your favourite.
card.good_to_know: Agios Stefanos means Saint Stephen. The beach is a sandy stretch beside Tourlos, the newer harbour of Mykonos. You can get there by regular bus from Mykonos town, or by taxi or private vehicle.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk to the far end of Agios Stefanos beach, about 3.5 km from Mykonos town, and stand at the front of the chapel facing the sea. From the sand, look south to spot the chapel. Keep it in the foreground and let the bay and Delos fill the background.

card.hook: Psarou is about as simple as a beach gets: a curve of sand, clear water and big yachts parked offshore like they own the place. That simplicity is why it photographs so well.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, on the public sand of Psarou Beach. Face the bay, away from the beach club loungers, so sunbeds and umbrellas stay out of your foreground.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the sand, water and yachts in one frame. Go 0.5x for more sea and sky, or 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out a single yacht.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the sea or a yacht, then slide it a touch darker so the bright sky and white sand don't wash out.
card.best_time: Come in late afternoon, when the light on the bay is warm and the yachts show up as dark shapes against the sea. For a calmer bay, go early in the morning, before the loungers fill the front of the beach from late morning.
card.selfie_here: Try the rock shelf on the eastern headland, on the Mykonos Blu side, where the rock drops toward the water. Use the front camera with the bay opening out behind you, ideally early, when the bay is calm and empty.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the small walking track up the hill above the beach and look down at the bay, while you stand in front of them.
card.rules_and_safety: The beach itself is public sand, but the beach club area is paid, so shoot from the public sand. The corner next to Mykonos Blu is also a reviewer's suggestion for a spot, and they say to ask the resort whether it can be paid for.
card.challenge: Put the horizon on a gridline, keep a strip of clean sand along the bottom, and park one yacht neatly on the water line. Bonus points if there isn't a single sunbed in it.
card.good_to_know: Psarou is a small village on Mykonos, set around a sheltered bay. It's about 4 km from Mykonos town (Chora) and close to Platys Gialos. It had a population of 106 as of 2021.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, on the public sand of Psarou Beach. Face the bay, away from the beach club loungers, so sunbeds and umbrellas stay out of your foreground.

card.hook: Most churches are neat. This one looks like someone sculpted it out of whipped cream and then let it set against the sky, all lumpy white curves.
card.stand_here: Start at the phone icon on the map, right at the Church of Panagia Paraportiani in Chora's Kastro neighbourhood. For the sea view, walk down and to the left of the church to the rocky outcrop on the seaward side, then turn to face the church with open sea behind it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the church with the sea behind it. From the rocks, try 0.5x to squeeze in Little Venice and the windmills, or 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) to pick out the windmills in the distance.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the white wall, then slide the brightness a little darker so the whitewash keeps its texture and the sky stays blue.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on white walls than midday. Take a few frames either way, as sea spray and passers-by can spoil a single shot.
card.selfie_here: Climb down a short way from the church's seaward edge to the rocky corner just below it, where the sea is the only backdrop. Use the front camera, tilt the phone up a touch and see if the church fits above your shoulder, since that angle is our best guess and worth checking on your screen.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand a few metres back on the small plaza facing the church, so the whole whitewashed building fits in the frame, while you stand in front of it.
card.rules_and_safety: The footing on the rocks can be uneven, and one visitor found broken glass and trash there, so watch your step. The inside of the church opens only at service times, so check locally.
card.challenge: Turn on gridlines, park the church's white mass on one side, let the sea fill the rest, and keep that horizon dead level. No wonky sea allowed!
card.good_to_know: It's really five churches in one: four at ground level form the base of a fifth built on top. Work began in 1425 and wasn't finished until the 17th century. The name means "Our Lady of the Side Gate", because the entrance was once by the side gate into the Kastro area.

card.hook: Everyone else on this beach is taking the same sand-and-sea shot. You get to put a village from around 5000 to 4500 BC in yours.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the phone icon, up on the low ruins on the small rise above the middle of Ftelia Beach, so there's no extra walk once you're there. Face the sea so the old stone walls sit in front of you and the beach and bay stretch out behind them.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the walls, beach and bay all in one frame. Try 0.5x if you want a low, sweeping foreground (keep the phone level so the horizon doesn't bend), or 2x to pick out a single wall without leaning into the ruins.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, crouch a little to put a stretch of wall in the bottom third, then tap the stones and slide the picture a touch darker so the sky and sea keep their colour.
card.best_time: Any time of day works here. If you can, pick a calmer spell, because the wind and dust can be strong.
card.selfie_here: Use the settlement walls above Ftelia Beach, with the ruins, beach and sea behind you for a mix of history and classic island scenery. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and keep the walls over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the steps up to the Ftelia Beach Bar while you stand on the beach below, so they can frame you with the whole beach spread out behind.
card.rules_and_safety: The site is still being excavated and large parts are closed, so stay on the marked paths and don't step into the dig area.
card.challenge: Get a wall in the bottom third, the sea along the top, and a horizon so straight your friends think you used a ruler.
card.good_to_know: Around 150 to 200 people are thought to have lived in this village. Diggers found pottery, stone tools, 19 small stone figurines and a circular gold object, thought to be the earliest securely dated gold from the Aegean. Keep your expectations modest: the walls are low, so treat them as a foreground detail rather than the main attraction.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the phone icon, up on the low ruins on the small rise above the middle of Ftelia Beach, so there's no extra walk once you're there. Face the sea so the old stone walls sit in front of you and the beach and bay stretch out behind them.

card.hook: Most of Mykonos is shouting at you to look at the sea. This pale, neat little museum just stands there looking calm, and that's why it photographs so well.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the phone icon on the map, near the Old Port, and face the museum entrance. If you want the whole front in the shot, step back along whatever space the street gives you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the front of the building. Switch to 0.5x only if the street is too narrow to step back, and go to 2x for the doorway and window frames. 0.5x can stretch the edges of the building, so use it sparingly.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the walls up with the vertical lines so they stay straight, then tap the pale wall and drag the slider to make it a little darker if the white looks too bright.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people in the street. Midday sun can make those white walls look harsh.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, hold your phone a little above eye level and keep the building over your shoulder. Try zoom 0.5x if your phone has it, so more of the building squeezes in behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography rules inside the museum can differ, so check the official site before you go. Take your exterior pictures from the street.
card.challenge: Take one dead-straight, perfectly level front shot, then one a little further back where the street makes the building feel part of the town. Which one wins?
card.good_to_know: The museum was established in 1902 by the Greek Archaeological Service, first to hold finds from a burial site on the nearby islet of Rineia (Rhenia). The original building dates from 1905, was refurbished and extended in the 1930s and 1960s, and got a large eastern room in 1972. Inside you'll find pottery, funerary urns and sculpture, and its best-known piece is the large Mykonos vase, which shows scenes from the fall of Troy.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the phone icon on the map, near the Old Port, and face the museum entrance. If you want the whole front in the shot, step back along whatever space the street gives you.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a selfie spot with the Archaeological Museum of Mykonos behind the visitor, or a spot where a passer-by should stand to photograph a visitor with the whole building in frame. Nothing was added from memory. The closest material: inmykonos.com (http://www.inmykonos.com/see-and-do-in-mykonos/museums/1514-archaeological-museum.html) describes the museum as on the road from the Old Port into town and says four free-standing pillars look majestic against the blue sea, but it does not say where to stand. Other pages (kupi.com, mykonosbeachesguide.com, daytripsfrommykonos.com) place the museum on the Old Port waterfront, but none of them names a photo position there. Several guides mention the Old Port and Little Venice as photo areas, but not for this museum. The only photography rule found is a museum rule, not a selfie-stick or tripod rule: kupi.com and airial.travel say non-flash personal photography is generally permitted and that signs should be checked. That does not meet the brief's rule criteria, so I left it out. Sources also disagree on the entry fee (1 EUR per daytripsfrommykonos.com, 4 EUR per usnews, free per iqcruising), which is not relevant to the selfie question but shows the pages are not fully consistent. A local photo-spot search or on-site check would be needed for this landmark.

card.hook: A full-size 1890 lighthouse in a garden in the middle of town? That's the Aegean Maritime Museum, and the tall, upright lighthouse makes it easy to build a photo around.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, right at the museum in the Tria Pigadia area of Mykonos Town. Face the lighthouse in the garden, and look around a bit for the cleanest view of the building and garden.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x if you're squeezed for space and want the building and garden in one go. Switch to 1x for a more natural look, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the top of the lighthouse and the carved gravestones.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the lighthouse up on one of the vertical lines, then hold your phone level so nothing leans.
card.best_time: Go in the morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer. Midday sun can wash out the detail. It's a museum, so check opening times locally before you go.
card.selfie_here: Take it in the museum's green garden courtyard with the Armenistis lighthouse behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to squeeze the lighthouse in over your shoulder, and tilt the phone up a little so the whole tower fits.
card.rules_and_safety: Photo rules can vary, so look for signs or ask the staff when you arrive before you start snapping.
card.challenge: Find an old marble gravestone, move in close, and try portrait mode so the garden turns soft and dreamy behind it.
card.good_to_know: The museum sits in a 19th-century Mykonian building, and the Armenistis Lighthouse in the garden was built in 1890. The garden also holds ancient sailors' marble gravestones gathered from Mykonos and Delos. The museum is a non-profit, founded in 1983 and open to the public since 1985, and it focuses on Greek maritime history, especially the merchant ships of the Aegean.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, right at the museum in the Tria Pigadia area of Mykonos Town. Face the lighthouse in the garden, and look around a bit for the cleanest view of the building and garden.

selfie_spots.why: The tranquil, green courtyard is named as a prime photo spot, and the garden's lighthouse is the most visible landmark to frame behind you.

card.hook: Picture a white marble bell tower, three bells and a few crosses, standing out clean against the sky above Ano Mera's village square. The square gives you room to step back, so the whole tower fits in one shot.
card.stand_here: Stand in the far corner of Ano Mera Square, facing the bell tower. The monastery is about 1 minute on foot from the square, to the north-west.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole tower with some sky around it. Want the bells and crosses up close? Try zoom 2x or more (higher zooms depend on your phone). If you go into the courtyard, zoom 0.5x fits the church facade in.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on your gridlines, line the tower up with a vertical line, and leave a little sky above the crosses.
card.best_time: Go in the late afternoon, when low light from the west falls on the marble. Aim to shoot about 30 minutes before the tower falls into full shade.
card.selfie_here: Use the far corner of the Ano Mera square, where the tower looks best in late-afternoon light. Switch to the front camera, turn so the tower is behind you, and check it shows on your screen before you tap. Try zoom 0.5x if your phone has it, to fit more in.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the western edge of the square, about 25 m back from the monastery entrance, and frame the tower against the late-afternoon sky, while you stand in the square with the monastery in view.
card.rules_and_safety: It's an active place of worship, so keep your flash off, skip photos during services (avoid Sunday morning), and ask first before photographing inside the church. Cover your shoulders and knees if you go in.
card.challenge: Get the tower dead straight on a gridline with just a sliver of sky above the crosses, then do it again with you grinning in front.
card.good_to_know: Panagia Tourliani is the monastery at the heart of Ano Mera, and its white marble bell tower is the part most visitors photograph. The courtyard and whitewashed church facade with red-shuttered details make a second, more intimate picture. You need to go into the monastery grounds for it, so check the entrance fee and opening hours locally before you go.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the far corner of Ano Mera Square, facing the bell tower. The monastery is about 1 minute on foot from the square, to the north-west.
